newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO proposes big arms cuts as sweetner for Russia.
newsitem.headline: NATO proposes big arms cuts as sweetner for Russia.

text.p: NATO put forward a proposal at conventional arms reduction talks in Vienna on Thursday in an attempt to sweeten the alliance's planned eastward expansion for Russia, which opposes the move.

"The alliance is prepared to take significant steps in this regard. Specifically, the total of future aggregate national ceilings of ground treaty limited equipment of (NATO's) 16 members will be significantly less under the adapted treaty," said the proposal, delivered to the body dealing with the treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe.

A western diplomat said the motion, which will go before a working group on Tuesday, was a symbol of NATO's political goodwill towards a Moscow government wary of NATO plans to take in former Warsaw Pact states.

"That is the key political signal of this proposal that the alliance is prepared to lower its overall force levels. We see this as unilateral steps. We say significantly so we are not talking about one or two percent here," the diplomat said.

Officials hope the new arms reduction proposal, which modifies the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty, will go a long way towards calming Russian fears that NATO could pile up weapons on its borders.

The Russians want a legally binding contract providing security guarantees. The Americans say the proposed modification of CFE, which is a treaty requiring ratification by 30 signatory states, amounts to that legally binding document.

The proposal also establishes a "sensitive geographic region" in central Europe comprising the Baltic enclave of Kaliningrad, Ukraine, Slovakia, Belarus, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland. It makes clear that ground equipment in that area cannot increase.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Albright, on her first trip to Moscow in her new post, will spell out the package to the Russian government on Thursday.

NATO leaders intend to issue formal invitations to the alliance's first new post-Cold War members at a July summit in Madrid. Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are the top contenders for membership.
